evals.prompt: I'm putting together the delivery plan for a hands-on Rust session at NordShift, our 400-person conference in Gothenburg. It runs three hours, 36 people have registered, and the exercise is one linear path at every seat: clone a repo, get it building, then work through four refactors in order. I've got four volunteers assigned to that room - two are venue stewards who mostly point people at the toilets, and two are engineers from our sponsor who have shipped Rust in anger. The instructor is one of our regulars. How many of them do I actually put in the room, and how do I justify the number to our volunteer lead, who wants them on registration instead?
evals.expected_output: A coverage decision that refuses a ratio, sizes from the exercise structure and the pool of material-competent people, lands on one instructor plus one roaming troubleshooter, states the sizing basis as the organizer's own, and names the condition that would change it.
expectations: States explicitly that there is no facilitator-to-participant ratio to apply, and refuses to produce one.
Produces no figure of the form 'one helper per N participants', and does not divide the 36 registrations by a helper count.
Sizes coverage from the structure of the exercise - how many distinct steps it has and who can debug each - rather than from the headcount.
Marks the coverage figure as the organizer's own judgment rather than an external standard or published benchmark.
Excludes the two venue stewards from the coverage count on the grounds that they are competent in logistics but not in the material.
Recommends a roaming troubleshooter as the default posture for this session.
Describes the roaming person as someone who could deliver the session themselves, not a general-purpose volunteer.
States that the roaming person's trigger is observing participants who are falling behind, not waiting for a raised hand.
Does not recommend running the session solo, and states that the solo option is struck rather than ranked last because the session is genuinely hands-on.
Gives the promotion condition for posting helpers at fixed points - the exercise runs at physically or logically distinct steps - and notes this exercise's single linear path does not meet it.
If structured pairing is proposed, it assigns a driver and a navigator and swaps the roles every five to ten minutes.
Names the failure where both members of a pair are stuck and produce no signal, and gives the fix of checking in with pairs on a regular cadence.
Decides and briefs what a helper is permitted to do to a participant's machine rather than leaving it to the helper on the day.

evals.prompt: Setting the seat cap for the embedded track at Kessler Devcon. The venue calls the room the Large Workshop Suite and says it seats 30. The furniture is fixed - long benches bolted to the floor - and power runs along two walls only. The exercise needs one dev board and one vendor toolchain login per participant: we own 9 boards, and the vendor issued us 20 logins. Registration opens Monday and marketing wants a number for the page today. What number do I give them, and what do I say when someone asks why it's that number?
evals.expected_output: Three ceilings computed separately, the lowest taken as capacity at 9 bound by the dev boards, with the room ceiling adjusted for fixed furniture and power, and the coverage ceiling stated with its sizing logic rather than a looked-up figure.
expectations: Computes three separate ceilings - room, coverage, and exercise throughput - rather than producing a single capacity number directly.
Takes the lowest of the three as the capacity.
States which ceiling bound the number.
Gives 9 as the capacity, bound by the number of dev boards.
Does not rank the three ceilings against each other or present them as alternatives with different value or efficiency.
Reduces the room ceiling below the venue's stated 30 seats because the benches are fixed, and treats power at the seats as a separate question from the seat count.
Infers no capacity from the room's name.
States the coverage ceiling with its sizing logic attached instead of a number looked up from a standard.
Notes that the throughput ceiling is the one invisible on the registration page until a participant is left without a device.
Hands the capacity figure onward as an input to scheduling rather than placing the session in the grid itself.
Invents no per-seat bandwidth or power figure specific to a workshop room; any per-attendee density figure used is labelled as an upper bound borrowed from hackathon-floor guidance.
If a pre-event demand vote is proposed for matching sessions to rooms, states that it ranks demand and lifts none of the three ceilings.

evals.prompt: Trying to fix the slot length for the hands-on sessions at Quarry Summit before the CFP text goes out. I pulled the published lengths from three conferences I respect: one ran theirs at 150 minutes, one at 180, and one had a session on its workshop page listed at 50 minutes called Find Your Team. That averages to about 127, so I was going to round to 120 and put that in the call. Our exercise has three parts plus a wrap-up. Does 120 hold up?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to average across events, the 45-minute granularity offered as the transferable pattern, the 50-minute instance excluded as a format with no exercise, and a length derived from this exercise's own segments plus recovery time, handed on to scheduling.
expectations: Rejects averaging published session lengths across different events.
States that each event's published length reflects its own rooms, cohort and exercise.
Does not endorse 120 minutes as a number derived from that average.
Offers 45-minute granularity as the transferable pattern rather than any single borrowed number.
Notes that published genuinely hands-on sessions cluster at 150-180 minutes, presented as an observation rather than a rule.
Excludes the 50-minute Find Your Team instance from the range on the grounds that it is a format with no exercise in it.
Derives the proposed length from this exercise's own segments plus recovery time rather than from the three benchmark events.
Schedules troubleshooting, breakout and question time explicitly inside the length rather than assuming it fits.
Hands the chosen length onward to scheduling as an input.
Does not place the session in the grid or size the buffer between sessions.
States that no relationship between session length and capacity can be derived from the published record.
Presents every length figure it uses as an observed instance rather than as a standard or an average.

evals.prompt: Here is the prerequisites text we published last year for the hands-on LLM session at Fernbank Devcon. It went badly and I want it rewritten before the page goes live on Friday. Current text, in full: 'Bring a laptop. Some familiarity with Python is helpful. We'll get everyone set up in the first 15 minutes.' This year the exercise runs against a hosted vendor console, needs a free account with that vendor plus a GitHub login, and pulls roughly 2 GB of container images. The session is 150 minutes, of which about 90 is meant to be hands-on.
evals.expected_output: A prerequisite block rewritten into prior knowledge, machine state and accounts, with the accounts class populated and flagged as highest risk, the setup-on-the-day promise removed, and a pre-download step added with its reason attached.
expectations: Rewrites the block into three labelled classes in this order: prior knowledge, machine state, accounts.
Includes an accounts class listing both the vendor account and the GitHub login.
Flags accounts as the highest-risk prerequisite class because signups, email confirmations and sometimes employer sign-on all land at minute zero, on the room's network, for everyone simultaneously.
Marks each prerequisite as a hard requirement or a comfort.

Replaces 'some familiarity with Python is helpful' with a hard capability statement, and states that the word 'helpful' drops the room's floor to zero and forces the instructor to address two audiences.
States prior knowledge as a capability rather than a job title or a seniority level.
Specifies in the machine-state class that the laptop must be one the participant is permitted to install software on.
Names the install route or links the tooling directly rather than leaving participants to find their own.
Removes the promise to set everyone up in the first 15 minutes, and names the simultaneous-install load that promise creates.
Adds a pre-travel step asking participants to pull the 2 GB of images on a network they trust, with the reason stated in the participant-facing text.
Publishes known failure modes participants can act on themselves, such as a corporate VPN or an ad blocker breaking the lab.
Publishes how long the materials stay reachable after the session, alongside a named follow-up channel.
Argues for keeping the account list as short as the exercise allows, because an account the participant created persists under their name after the event and the organizer cannot delete it for them.

evals.prompt: We have partnered with two upper schools to bring 20 students, most of them 16 or 17, to the hands-on day at Tallow Conf. Their school laptops are locked down: no admin rights, no installs, and the IT departments will not budge. One of our sponsors has offered to stand up their browser-based cloud IDE for the whole room, free, with an individual login per student. That feels like it solves everything at once. What am I missing before I say yes?
evals.expected_output: The provisioned-environment rung promoted with its condition named, its trade stated rather than treated as safe, the compliance review and credential-holding questions named, the minors question routed rather than answered, and the network posture escalated.
expectations: Promotes provisioned-environment-only and states the promotion condition: participants are not permitted to install software on the machines they bring.
Refuses to treat the provisioned environment as the safe option, and names what it trades for: total dependence on the room's connection for the whole session.
Names the review triggered by accepting a third-party platform's terms on behalf of a room of people who never read them.
Treats the per-student logins as participant data, with a stated position on who may hold them and for how long.
Routes the question of minors rather than answering it, because the acceptance is being made for someone who cannot make it themselves.
Routes the participant-data posture to the event's accessibility and inclusion work rather than inventing one here.
States the reversibility asymmetry: an environment is torn down on the organizer's schedule, while an account a participant created persists afterwards.
Requires the environment's preinstalled toolchain versions to be published, so a participant can tell whether it matches a tutorial they follow later.
Publishes the window after the session during which the environment stays reachable.
Escalates the network posture because the whole session now depends on the room's connection, rather than leaving the connection as an assumption.
Does not present offering a local path alongside the provisioned one as free, and names that it creates two environments and two support surfaces.
Still publishes a machine-state prerequisite, such as a specific modern browser, rather than stating that nothing is required of the laptop.
States that the sponsor providing the environment removes neither the terms review nor the credential-holding question.

evals.prompt: Our hands-on security session at Broadleaf Summit needs participants to RDP into a Windows jump host and hit a hosted console for the whole 150 minutes. I asked the venue about the network and got one line back: 'We have fast fibre WiFi throughout, no problem.' Two years ago at the same venue the hands-on room fell over about twenty minutes in and we never worked out why. We are seven weeks out and the page is already live. What do I do?
evals.expected_output: The venue's assurance refused, three written questions put to them, policy named as the likely cause with specific mechanisms, the pre-download ask added, removing the live dependency promoted on the prior failure, and the hands-on option struck if no written answer arrives.
expectations: Rejects 'we have fast fibre WiFi throughout, no problem' as an answer and requires a written answer to specific questions.
Asks the venue how many simultaneous devices the room's access point holds and what happens at that limit.
Asks the venue which protocols and ports are blocked, and whether they can be opened for the day.
Asks the venue whether unusual device classes are blocked by default and who can grant an exception on the day.
Identifies policy rather than bandwidth as the likelier cause of the failure.
Names specific policy causes: a blocked protocol such as RDP, a blocked device class, a participant's own VPN, and an ad blocker.
Treats a room of simultaneous cold installs or downloads as a load case and asks participants to pre-download beforehand.
Removes 'assume the network holds' from consideration rather than ranking it last.
Promotes removing the live dependency on the strength of the prior edition's failure at the same venue.
States that if the venue will not answer in writing, the hands-on option is struck and the session runs as a demonstration with the material published.
States that the venue failing to answer is itself the evidence, not a missing input to keep waiting on.
Declares the dependency in the published prerequisites and names a participant-side fallback such as tethering to their own data.
Routes the live, mid-session response to a network failure to the event's run of show rather than improvising a protocol here.

evals.prompt: Kafka workshop at Highfield Conf, eight weeks out. The exercise streams from a hosted cluster and there is no offline version of it - the whole point is watching real consumer lag. I have emailed the venue three times about the network and heard nothing back. I still want to run it hands-on and just have a fallback plan ready in case things go wrong on the day. What should the fallback be?
evals.expected_output: The full hands-on option struck rather than kept with a fallback, a demonstration plus published material recommended as the actual plan, and the async material designed as a layer with formats and an availability window.
expectations: Strikes the full hands-on option entirely rather than keeping it with a fallback attached.
States that an option left ranked at the bottom reappears as scope on the day.
Recommends running the session as a demonstration with the material published.
Treats publishing the material with no live exercise as a legitimate outcome rather than a failure or a climbdown.
Notes that the no-live-exercise option wins on efficiency because nothing in it can fail on the day.
Names the condition that would have justified full hands-on: the capability cannot be acquired by reading the material.
Does not reopen whether the workshop day should exist or how it is priced, and routes that decision elsewhere as already made.
Asks what a participant must be able to do at the end that they cannot do now.

Treats the async material as a designed layer, pairing content types with formats: short video for skills demonstrations, a graphic-heavy document for procedures, and a repository for anything participants copy from.
Publishes the material with a stated availability window.
Does not propose a mobile hotspot, a second connection or purchased bandwidth as a substitute for the missing written answer.
States that the venue's silence is the promotion condition for removing the live dependency.

evals.prompt: Give me the options for getting a stuck participant unstuck during the hands-on sessions at Marlowe Devdays, ranked, so I know what to do first. Context you'll want: our instructor runs this exact workshop commercially about once a month, so she has seen every way it breaks. Rooms hold 25 to 30 people. We have budget to bring in one extra person, not four. First edition is in five months and if it lands we will run it every year after that.
evals.expected_output: Per-axis orderings with structured peer pairing leading on efficiency, the recovery-latency axis flagged as rank-identical to inverse effort, the starved option named with its promotion condition, and a re-rank against the commercially experienced instructor.
expectations: Emits a separate ordering line per axis - effort, value, efficiency - rather than one blended ranking.
Names structured peer pairing as the efficiency leader.
Does not place the solo instructor at the top of the efficiency ordering on the grounds that it is the cheapest.
Justifies peer pairing's lead by the fact that its help capacity grows with the size of the room.
Flags that ordering the options by how fast a stuck participant is reached is rank-identical to inverse effort and therefore discriminates nothing.
Argues the tie between the roaming option and the solo option on the growth axis rather than using the tie to avoid deciding.
Names what the efficiency ordering starves - the option high on value and high on effort - and states the condition that promotes it anyway.
States that the ranking is a default rather than a law, and that it shifts with context and with who executes it.
Asks the delivery date, whether this is a one-off or a recurring curriculum, and the effort ceiling before presenting the ranking.
Re-ranks against the instructor who already runs this workshop commercially, and says which stated fact moved which option.
Expresses effort and value without any currency amount and without numeric scores or fixed tier counts.
Does not recommend solo delivery for a 25-to-30-person hands-on room.

evals.prompt: Our board wants proof the training day at Ashgrove Conf was worth what we spent. Somebody suggested we just run NPS on it the way we do for the main conference. I would rather measure something real. Six hands-on sessions across the day, roughly 25 people in each. What do we measure, and what numbers should we be aiming for?
evals.expected_output: Two or three metrics with a revision trigger written for each in advance, the pre-and-post confidence pair identified as the one with a named precedent and caveated, other metrics labelled self-set, and a refusal to supply target figures.
expectations: Recommends two or three metrics rather than a full dashboard.
Writes down for each metric, before the session runs, what result would change the next edition.
Labels which metrics are self-set and which carry a published precedent.
Proposes a confidence rating on the specific skill taught, asked before the session and again at the end, as the metric with a named precedent.
Refuses to supply target numbers to aim for, and presents no published confidence figure as a target to hit.
Caveats the confidence precedent: it comes from life-sciences and data-science training and measures self-reported confidence rather than observed task completion.
Includes the share of the room that arrived with the prerequisites already done, and states that the only way to get it is to ask at the door.
Includes how many participants reached the last exercise, and reads a wide gap in a full room as a coverage problem and in a small room as a prerequisites problem.
Notes that how long a raised hand waits is deliberately not the axis the facilitator choice rests on.
Includes use of the published material inside the announced window as the honest test of whether the room was needed at all.
Excludes sell-through of the separately ticketed training day and routes it to the format decision.

evals.prompt: Post-mortem time. Our workshop day at Penhale Conf was a mess. The room's network died about 25 minutes into the first session and never really came back. The camera feed on the recorded session dropped twice, so the video is unusable. Two of the four parallel sessions were scheduled to end 15 minutes apart, which jammed the corridor both times. And half the team now thinks we should stop charging separately for the day. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: The attendee-side failure separated from production and scheduling failures and routed accordingly, the pricing question declined, the network cause interrogated before any fix, and a delivery sheet produced section by section for the parts owned here.
expectations: Separates the attendee-side network failure, which it owns, from the dropped camera feed, which it does not.
Routes the unusable recording to the event's production work.
Routes the two sessions ending 15 minutes apart to schedule design.
Routes the question of charging separately for the day to the format decision and does not re-argue it.
Asks what specifically broke on the network - sustained bandwidth, a blocked protocol, a blocked device class, or the venue never answering - before proposing a fix.
Treats that answer as the promotion condition for next edition's network posture rather than jumping straight to a remedy.
Does not propose more bandwidth as the fix without first establishing whether the cause was policy.

Produces a per-session delivery sheet for the parts it owns, covering the hands-on commitment, the capacity and which ceiling bound it, coverage with its sizing basis, prerequisites, the network posture, the materials and their window, and the revision trigger per choice.
Presents that output section by section for validation rather than as a single block.
Records for the next edition which ceiling bound capacity, the prerequisite sheet as shipped, what actually broke on the day, and the venue's written network answer.
Does not re-decide whether the workshop day should exist.

evals.prompt: Small one. Twelve people, two hours, hands-on session on our internal tracing tooling at Corvid Conf. The instructor is our principal engineer - genuinely brilliant - but three people told me after last year's edition that they did not want to ask him anything in front of the room. Most of the attendees this time are juniors who have never been to a conference before. What do I do with the session itself?
evals.expected_output: In-room mechanics sized to a small first-timer room: an icebreaker, an explicit normalisation of being stuck placed on the instructor, scheduled troubleshooting time, a deliberate close with a follow-up channel and published windows, delivered as a per-session sheet.
expectations: Recommends opening with an icebreaker, keyed to the small size of the room.
States no participant count that defines when a room is small.
Puts an explicit sentence at the front of the session normalising being stuck - that anyone hitting an issue almost certainly is not alone in the room.
Names the intimidation of questions and review in front of the room as the specific thing being addressed, and puts the responsibility for it on the instructor.
Prompts participants for active participation explicitly rather than assuming it happens.
Builds troubleshooting and question time into the plan as scheduled time rather than hoping it fits inside the two hours.
Closes the session deliberately and keeps the instructor available to attendees afterwards rather than leaving with their laptop.
Opens a follow-up channel for the topic and publishes how long it stays open.
Publishes how long the materials stay reachable.
Does not recommend a solo instructor for the exercise portion despite the small room.

Delivers a per-session sheet covering the hands-on commitment with its reason, the capacity and which ceiling bound it, coverage with its sizing basis, prerequisites split into prior knowledge, machine state and accounts, the network posture, the materials and their window, and the revision trigger for each choice.
